Fourteen years. That is how long Nuevo Laredo's business and civic leaders say they have been asking for a new IMSS hospital — a request that dates back to 2012 and has now, at last, reached the point where land is secured and only the money is missing.

According to the Consejo de Instituciones, the city's business federation, members have petitioned all three levels of government since 2012 for a new Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) hospital, because the current General Hospital is simply too small for the population it must serve. The group's president, Francisco Mejía Barrientos, is himself a physician, and he frames the problem in blunt clinical terms: demand is rising and the building is saturated.

Mejía Barrientos says the new hospital would finally give the institute in Nuevo Laredo room for the third-level specialties the IMSS already provides there — oncologic surgery, renal surgery, cardiology and gastroenterology. The point, he says, is that patients should not have to be transferred to Monterrey, Reynosa, Tampico or other cities that do have third-level care. His own hospital, he notes, has already handled cardiovascular procedures requiring 10 to 12 units of plasma and blood — proof, in his telling, that the talent exists and only the facility is missing.

He also raised a staffing warning that deserves attention: good doctors, he said, do not come to work at the IMSS for low pay, and the institute will need real outreach and flexible agreements with physicians if a bigger, more specialized hospital is to be staffed at all. The patient volume is huge and the salaries are small, in his words.

The numbers behind the demand are striking. The saturated facility serves roughly 75,000 direct insured persons — and once family members and pensioners are counted, the figure climbs to nearly 300,000 people in Nuevo Laredo alone. Across Tamaulipas, the institute covers approximately 2 million derechohabientes.

The latest development: a new IMSS hospital for the city has reportedly been authorized, with a five-hectare lot donated by the municipal government, a plan for 120 beds, and a design that could grow from second-level care to third-level care over time. The land, in other words, is ready. The budget is not.

One detail in the original report demands a closer look. The published figure for the investment — approximately 1.8 million pesos — is implausibly small for a 120-bed hospital and almost certainly a reporting error (likely millions vs. billions). That is exactly the kind of figure citizens should watch: a 14-year request, a donated site, and a price tag that does not add up. If Nuevo Laredo is going to wait on this hospital, it deserves an accurate number on the check.

Sources: Manifiesto Tamaulipas, "Petición de un nuevo hospital del IMSS tiene 14 años, asegura el Consejo de Instituciones" (October 21, 2026) — https://manifiestotamaulipas.com/2026/10/21/peticion-de-un-nuevo-hospital-del-imss-tiene-14-anos-segura-el-consejo-de-instituciones/

title: 14 Years Waiting: Nuevo Laredo's New IMSS Hospital Has Land — But Not the Money
